title: Confidentiality with young people and when it must be broken
blurb: Keep a young person's confidence, explain its limits honestly, and share safeguarding information under the s16LA duty when you must.
question: Nadia, 16, tells a ward nurse that her stepfather is sexually abusing her 11-year-old sister. She begs the nurse to tell no one. What should the nurse do?

teach.h: Young people are owed confidence too
teach.body: A young person is owed the same duty of confidence as an adult. A competent 15-year-old's sexual health care, or a 16-year-old's reason for admission, is not shared with parents without their agreement. The NMC Code (5.4) allows information to be shared when the interests of patient safety and public protection override the need for confidentiality. In plain English: privacy is the default, but a child's safety comes first.

children.edge: Risk of harm to them or another child
children.label: Share for safeguarding

teach.body: When a child says 'promise you won't tell', the honest answer is that you cannot promise, but you will share only with people who need to know to help keep them safe. Explaining the limits of confidentiality at the start of a consultation, especially a psychosocial history with a teenager, builds trust and avoids a broken promise later.

teach.h: The s16LA information sharing duty (from 30 Sept 2026)
head: Feature
What the duty says
rows: Relevant persons: LAs, ICBs, NHS trusts, GPs, police, schools
Information relevant to safeguarding or promoting welfare
None: early help and unmet need included
Disclosure does not breach any obligation of confidence
Sharing would be more detrimental to the child
teach.caption: Children Act 2004 s16LA, inserted by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026; statutory guidance September 2026.

teach.h: Sharing with agencies vs telling parents
teach.caption: s16LA is a duty to share with other relevant persons, not a licence to share a competent young person's care with family.

teach.body: The September 2026 guidance says consent is not required for sharing under the duty, and practitioners should avoid seeking consent if they intend to share anyway: asking implies the young person's 'no' would stop it. Instead, where it is safe, explain what will be shared, with whom and why. Do not tell the family first if that could put the child at risk. A worry about a complaint, or a parent being unhappy, is not a reason to withhold.
teach.cite: Information Sharing Duty statutory guidance, Sept 2026, paras 11, 42-44

teach.h: Applying it: Nadia and her sister
teach.body: The nurse cannot keep this secret: an 11-year-old is at risk of sexual abuse. She tells Nadia kindly that she must share it to keep her sister safe, explains who will be told, and reassures her she did the right thing. She informs the safeguarding lead and refers to children's social care that day, sharing what is relevant without Nadia's consent, and records what was shared, with whom, when and why. Nadia is offered support too.

teach.text: The old 'seven golden rules' are not the current framework in England. Since 30 September 2026, safeguarding information is shared under the s16LA duty: no threshold, no consent needed, and sharing does not breach confidence. The sole exception is where sharing would be more detrimental to the child than not sharing.

items: Young people are owed the same duty of confidence as adults; competent young people control who in the family knows.
Never promise secrecy; explain limits at the start.
Share where a child is at risk of harm, or to prevent serious harm to others.
s16LA (from 30 Sept 2026): share relevant safeguarding information with relevant persons; no threshold; consent not required; no breach of confidence.
Exception: sharing more detrimental to the child than not sharing.
Be transparent where safe; record what, with whom, when and why.

summary: You can now keep a young person's confidence, explain its limits, and recognise when it must be broken. You can also apply the s16LA duty: share safeguarding information without consent or threshold, transparently and with a clear record.

A.q: Kai, 10, says during a dressing change, 'I'll tell you something about my uncle, but you have to promise not to tell anyone.' What is the best response?
options: 'I promise, so you can tell me anything you like.'
'I can't promise, but I'll only share it to keep you safe.'
'Tell your mum first, and then I'll listen to you.'
'I need to fetch the safeguarding nurse before you say more.'
A.why: You cannot promise secrecy. Explaining honestly that you would share only with people who can help keeps trust and leaves the door open.

whyNot.0: A promise you may have to break damages trust.
whyNot.2: Sending him to his mother may silence him or put him at risk.
whyNot.3: Stopping him before he speaks may lose the disclosure; listen first.

A.q: Isla, 14, is judged competent and asks the school nurse not to tell her parents she has asked for help with severe acne. There are no safeguarding concerns. What should the nurse do?
options: Tell her parents, as she is under 16
Tell her parents if they ask about the visit
Keep it confidential, as she is owed confidence
Share it with her form tutor so the school can support her
A.why: A competent young person is owed the same duty of confidence as an adult. With no risk of harm, there is no reason to override it.

whyNot.0: Being under 16 does not remove confidentiality.
whyNot.1: A parent's question does not override her confidence.
whyNot.3: Sharing with a tutor breaches confidence without need.

A.q: From 30 September 2026, what does the s16LA duty require of an NHS children's nurse holding information relevant to a child's safety?
options: Share it with relevant agencies; consent is not required
Share it once the parents have given their consent
Share it once the s47 threshold has been confirmed
Share it if the child is Gillick competent and agrees to the sharing
A.why: s16LA requires relevant persons to share information relevant to safeguarding or welfare with other relevant persons. No threshold applies and consent is not required.

whyNot.1: Consent is not required under the duty.
whyNot.2: There is no statutory threshold before sharing.
whyNot.3: The child's agreement is not the basis for sharing under the duty.

B.q: Zoe, 16, has capacity and is admitted with an ectopic pregnancy. She asks staff not to tell her mother why she is in hospital. Her mother phones the ward. What is the best response?
options: Explain the reason, as her mother holds parental responsibility
Explain you can't share details, and pass on a message
Explain the reason, as Zoe is under 18
Explain that Zoe is not on the ward
B.why: Zoe is 16 with capacity and is owed confidence. The nurse does not disclose details without her agreement but can pass on a message.

whyNot.0: PR does not entitle a parent to a capable 16-year-old's confidential information.
whyNot.2: Being under 18 does not remove her right to confidence.
whyNot.3: Lying about her presence is dishonest; declining to give details is enough.

B.q: Ryan, 17, tells the nurse calmly and in detail that when discharged he will stab a named boy. What should the nurse do?
options: Keep it confidential, as Ryan is 17
Ask Ryan for consent before telling anyone
Record it in the notes and review it at the next ward round
Share with police and safeguarding to prevent harm
B.why: A specific threat of serious violence to another person justifies sharing to prevent harm (NMC Code 5.4), and the named boy is a child at risk.

whyNot.0: Age does not protect a threat of serious harm to others.
whyNot.1: Consent is not needed to share to prevent serious harm.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a ward round delays protection.

B.q: A practice nurse plans to share concerns about Leo, 5, with children's social care under s16LA. She intends to share whatever the parents say. How should she approach the parents?
options: Ask for their consent, so they feel involved
Share without telling them, as consent is not needed
Explain openly what will be shared and why
Ask their consent and share if they refuse
B.why: The guidance says do not seek consent if you will share anyway; instead, where safe, be open about what will be shared and why.

whyNot.0: Asking for consent you will not respect is misleading.
whyNot.1: Transparency is expected where it is safe.
whyNot.3: Asking then overriding a refusal is the practice the guidance warns against.

C.q: Yasmin, 13, lives in a refuge with her mother after fleeing domestic abuse. Another agency asks the school nurse for Yasmin's new address, and the nurse fears it could reach her father. When does the s16LA duty not require sharing?
options: When the father holds parental responsibility for her
When the information is held on paper
When the nurse is uncertain about the law
When sharing would be more detrimental to her
C.why: The duty does not apply where sharing would be more detrimental to the child than not sharing, for example where it would place her at immediate risk of harm.

whyNot.0: Holding PR does not create an exception under s16LA.
whyNot.1: The format of the record is irrelevant.
whyNot.2: Uncertainty is not a reason to withhold; seek advice.

C.q: Mia, 11, has possible neglect concerns. Her mother says she will complain if anything is shared with Mia's school. The ward nurse feels anxious. What is the best action?
options: Seek prompt advice from the safeguarding lead and share as needed
Withhold the information until the complaint is resolved
Share with the school after the mother has agreed to it in writing first
Ask Mia whether she would like her school to be told
C.why: The guidance says information must still be shared where the concern is a lack of consent, a parent's unhappiness or fear of complaint. The safeguarding lead can support the decision.

whyNot.1: Fear of complaint is not a reason to withhold.
whyNot.2: Parental agreement is not required for safeguarding sharing.
whyNot.3: Placing the decision on Mia is inappropriate; consent is not the basis.

C.q: After sharing safeguarding information about Ruby, 3, with her health visitor and social care, what should the nurse document?
options: That the parents consented to the sharing
What was shared, with whom, when and why
A summary of the outcome of the referral
That the seven golden rules were followed
C.why: Good practice is a clear record of what was shared, with whom, when and the reason for sharing.

whyNot.0: Consent is not the basis for safeguarding sharing.
whyNot.2: The outcome may not be known; the decision and content must be recorded now.
whyNot.3: The seven golden rules are not the current framework.

reteach.title: Private, until safety says otherwise
reteach.question: How do I balance confidence and safety with a young person?

blocks.body: The default is confidentiality, even from parents, for a competent young person. The override is safety: risk of harm to them, to another child, or serious harm to others. Since 30 September 2026 the s16LA duty makes safeguarding sharing with other agencies a legal duty: no threshold, no consent, no breach of confidence, unless sharing would harm the child more.

blocks.text: Never promise secrecy. Don't ask consent you won't honour. Record what, with whom, when, why.

explain.body: Young people are owed the same duty of confidence as adults. A competent young person decides whether parents are told about their care.

test.q: Sam, 15, is competent and receiving treatment for an eating disorder. His father asks for a copy of his notes. Sam does not want this. What should the nurse do?
options: Respect Sam's wishes and explain to his father
Give a summary instead of the full notes
Give the notes, as his father holds PR
Give the notes once the consultant in charge has agreed
test.why: A competent young person is owed confidence and decides who sees their information, absent a safety reason to override it.

whyNot.1: A summary still breaches his confidence.
whyNot.2: PR does not override a competent young person's confidence.
whyNot.3: Consultant agreement does not remove Sam's right to confidence.

explain.body: Explain at the start that what is said stays private unless someone is at risk of harm. Never promise secrecy.

test.q: Before taking a psychosocial history from Ruby, 15, what should the nurse say about confidentiality?
options: What stays private, and when sharing may be needed
Her parents will receive a summary
Everything she says will stay private
That it is best discussed later, to avoid making her anxious
test.why: Explaining both confidentiality and its limits builds trust and avoids a broken promise.

whyNot.1: A competent 15-year-old's history is not routinely shared with parents.
whyNot.2: Promising total privacy may have to be broken.
whyNot.3: Delaying leaves her unable to make an informed choice about what to share.

explain.body: Relevant persons must share information relevant to safeguarding or promoting a child's welfare with other relevant persons. No threshold; consent not required; no breach of confidence.

test.q: A health visitor has low-level concerns about Kai, 18 months, that would not meet a child protection threshold. Does the s16LA duty apply?
options: No, it applies at the s47 threshold
No, it applies once a referral is accepted
Yes, as no threshold must first be met
Yes, if the mother agrees to the sharing
test.why: The duty has no statutory threshold and covers early help and unmet need as well as child protection.

whyNot.0: The duty is not linked to the s47 threshold.
whyNot.1: Acceptance of a referral is not a precondition.
whyNot.3: Consent is not required under the duty.

explain.body: The duty does not apply where sharing would be more detrimental to the child than not sharing, for example placing the child at immediate risk. Such decisions should be rare and recorded.

test.q: Which reason, on its own, justifies not sharing under the s16LA duty?
options: The parent has refused consent
The family may make a complaint
The information was first reported by a neighbour
Sharing would put the child at immediate risk
test.why: The exception is where sharing would be more detrimental to the child, such as placing them at immediate risk of harm.

whyNot.0: Lack of consent is not a reason to withhold.
whyNot.1: Fear of complaint is not a reason to withhold.
whyNot.2: The source does not matter: information held about a child that is relevant to their welfare is within the duty.
